factor_ratings.evidence: Methodology is the mandatory sign-off gate for CTS closure across every NX-400 and NX-500 physical design handoff — impact spans the business unit's product lines, not just one team or function.
Owns the methodology outright as the sign-off authority company-wide; sets the standard others must comply with, accountable for outcomes without oversight described.
Skew-budgeting and CTS closure across multiple product generations involves competing constraints (timing, power, variability) but is a well-scoped technical domain, not open-ended strategic framing.
Deep authority in one narrow methodology area (CTS/skew-budgeting); explicitly 'has never worked outside this one methodology area' — no cross-disciplinary breadth described.

Owns a methodology/process used as mandatory gate across two product lines (NX-400, NX-500) — a major cross-product process, but not full platform or roadmap ownership across product lines' architecture.

Methodology mandates compliance from every physical design team doing CTS closure company-wide, indicating function-level and cross-team influence, but no evidence of executive or industry-level influence.

decision.governing_rule: rule 3: deep-but-narrow technical work caps at L5
decision.alternative_reasoning: If scope of impact were treated as unambiguously dominant per rule 1's tiebreaker guidance (mandatory gate across all NX-400/500 handoffs, company-wide), L6 could be argued. But rule 3 explicitly overrides scope-driven elevation when the work is deep-but-narrow with no cross-domain breadth or broader organizational influence, which is squarely the case here. L6 was not chosen because the narrow, single-methodology profile fails the breadth and influence requirements for that level.
decision.escalation_factor: technical_depth_breadth vs. scope_of_impact -- whether the company-wide mandatory sign-off authority constitutes sufficient organizational influence to overcome the narrow-breadth cap
decision.reasoning: The role shows strong scope-of-impact signals (mandatory company-wide sign-off gate across two product lines) that could point toward L6. However, the JD is explicit that this person has never worked outside this one methodology area — no cross-domain breadth — and has no patents or external publications. Per rule 3, deep-but-narrow technical work without cross-domain breadth and organizational influence caps at L5 regardless of how broad the ownership of that narrow area is. There's also no external recognition (rule 4 required for L7+, moot here but confirms no path above L6 anyway). Influence is real but confined to enforcing a single methodology's compliance, not cross-functional strategic alignment or executive credibility. So despite scope_of_impact evidence trending toward L6, the technical depth/breadth cap governs and the role is leveled at L5. Ownership scope (5a) reflects owning a subsystem-level methodology/process across product lines, consistent with L5's 'major subsystem' anchor rather than L6's 'architecture for a product line across generations.'
